airport: large aviation area with visible runways, terminal-like facilities, and broad paved zones, distinguishing airport from parking by lacking dense parked-vehicle rows, from farmland by lacking regular crop parcels, and from railwaystation by lacking concentrated rail-line structure.
bareland: broad exposed ground with barren surface and little vegetation, distinguishing bareland from desert by showing more mixed earth texture, from mountain by lacking strong relief and ridge shadows, and from farmland by lacking regular cultivated parcel boundaries.
baseballfield: compact sports field with a clear baseball-diamond layout and central infield geometry, distinguishing baseballfield from stadium by lacking a large enclosed spectator structure, from park by showing explicit game-field organization, and from playground by lacking generalized play-space layout.
beach: bright shoreline area with clear sand-water boundary and elongated coastal texture, distinguishing beach from river by lacking a narrow winding channel, from desert by showing direct coastal water contact, and from resort by having less organized leisure-oriented built infrastructure.
bridge: narrow man-made crossing structure spanning water or land, distinguishing bridge from river by being a discrete crossing rather than a continuous watercourse, from viaduct by showing a shorter localized span, and from pond by lacking a compact enclosed water body.
center: dense urban core with concentrated buildings and organized city-block structure, distinguishing center from stadium by lacking a dominant arena field, from church by lacking a single landmark-like religious complex, and from commercial by appearing as a broader civic core rather than distributed business blocks.
church: prominent religious building or complex with distinctive central architecture and surrounding open space, distinguishing church from center by emphasizing a landmark-like structure, from parking by lacking large open vehicle rows, and from school by lacking campus-style academic and sports organization.
commercial: organized business district with dense building blocks, roads, and urban infrastructure, distinguishing commercial from center by stronger business-block regularity, from industrial by lacking heavy factory-style compounds, and from parking by having dominant buildings rather than open paved vehicle space.
denseresidential: tightly packed residential roofs with very high housing density and minimal open spacing, distinguishing denseresidential from mediumresidential by much closer building intervals, from parking by showing repeated housing roofs instead of open paved lots, and from forest by lacking continuous tree canopy.
desert: wide sandy or arid region with homogeneous barren texture and very little vegetation, distinguishing desert from bareland by stronger sand-like continuity, from forest by lacking dense canopy, and from beach by lacking a clear shoreline water boundary.
farmland: regular cultivated land with organized field parcels and crop texture, distinguishing farmland from meadow by stronger parcel boundaries, from industrial by lacking dense factory compounds, and from pond by lacking a compact water body.
forest: dense continuous tree canopy with dark green natural texture and little visible built structure, distinguishing forest from desert by lacking barren sandy texture, from mountain by weaker relief and ridge shadows, and from denseresidential by lacking repeated roof patterns.
industrial: large factory-like compounds with utilitarian building layouts, storage yards, and production infrastructure, distinguishing industrial from storagetanks by not being dominated by circular tank clusters, from farmland by lacking regular cultivated parcels, and from railwaystation by lacking concentrated rail-line patterns.
meadow: broad natural grass-covered open area with soft vegetation texture and weak structural boundaries, distinguishing meadow from farmland by lacking regular agricultural parcels, from pond by being land-dominant rather than water-dominant, and from baseballfield by lacking explicit sports-field geometry.
mediumresidential: moderately spaced residential buildings with visible streets and yards, distinguishing mediumresidential from denseresidential by larger spacing between houses, from sparseresidential by denser neighborhood grouping, and from resort by showing a more regular residential layout rather than leisure-oriented organization.
mountain: rugged elevated terrain with strong relief, slope shadows, and irregular topographic structure, distinguishing mountain from forest by more obvious elevation variation, from bareland by stronger terrain relief, and from desert by less homogeneous arid surface texture.
park: planned green open space with vegetation, paths, and leisure-oriented spatial organization, distinguishing park from pond by being land-dominant rather than water-dominant, from square by stronger vegetation presence, and from baseballfield by lacking a dedicated diamond sports layout.
parking: large open paved area with organized parking spaces and vehicle-oriented rows, distinguishing parking from airport by lacking runways and aviation facilities, from port by lacking dock-water infrastructure, and from church by lacking a dominant landmark building.
playground: recreational activity area with sports or play surfaces and open activity layout, distinguishing playground from school by focusing on play-space geometry rather than full campus structure, from stadium by lacking a large enclosed spectator venue, and from baseballfield by lacking a diamond infield layout.
pond: small enclosed water body with compact water shape and visible boundary, distinguishing pond from river by lacking a long continuous winding channel, from park by emphasizing a central water region, and from farmland by lacking cultivated parcel texture.
port: waterfront transport area with docks, vessels, and shore-adjacent logistics structure, distinguishing port from parking by the presence of water and dock organization, from industrial by stronger harbor-water context, and from beach by denser man-made coastal infrastructure.
railwaystation: transport hub with concentrated rail lines and station-related structures, distinguishing railwaystation from industrial by stronger railway pattern organization, from parking by lacking large open vehicle lots, and from airport by lacking long aviation runways and aircraft-related paved regions.
resort: leisure-oriented built environment with organized open spaces and accommodation-like structures, distinguishing resort from beach by stronger built tourism layout, from mediumresidential by a more leisure-oriented spatial arrangement, and from pond by not being dominated by a compact water body.
river: elongated natural watercourse with continuous winding channel and visible banks, distinguishing river from pond by its longer linear flow shape, from bridge by being a natural channel rather than a crossing structure, and from beach by lacking a broad coastal shoreline.
school: campus-like area with multiple institutional buildings, open grounds, and organized academic layout, distinguishing school from playground by broader campus organization, from parking by stronger building and campus structure, and from park by more institutional spatial arrangement.
sparseresidential: widely separated residential houses with large open gaps and low housing density, distinguishing sparseresidential from mediumresidential by much larger spacing, from forest by showing repeated roof structures instead of continuous canopy, and from pond by lacking a water-dominant region.
square: open civic plaza-like space embedded in an urban area, distinguishing square from park by weaker vegetation dominance, from center by stronger central openness, and from parking by lacking organized vehicle rows.
stadium: large sports complex with prominent field or arena and surrounding spectator-related structure, distinguishing stadium from baseballfield by larger scale and venue enclosure, from center by emphasizing a dedicated sports facility, and from playground by stronger stadium-like structural framing.
storagetanks: clusters of large circular storage tanks with highly regular round geometry, distinguishing storagetanks from industrial by stronger circular-container dominance, from pond by lacking natural water appearance, and from center by lacking dense urban block organization.
viaduct: elongated elevated transport structure with clear grade-separated roadway form, distinguishing viaduct from bridge by its more extended raised-traffic pattern, from parking by lacking flat vehicle rows, and from playground by lacking sports or play-ground geometry.
